title: Order Types (Market, Limit, Stops)
objectives: Tell the difference between market, limit, and stop orders - and when each one gets you rekt
Understand why a market order pays a taker fee while a resting limit order earns a maker fee
See how order type choice changes your fill price, slippage, and total cost
Read a live order book well enough to place an order with intent instead of vibes

steps.title: Three Ways to Enter a Trade
steps.body:
Every trade you ever make is one of three instructions: get me in **now** (<Term id="market_order">market order</Term>), get me in **only at my price** (<Term id="limit_order">limit order</Term>), or get me out **if it breaks this level** (<Term id="stop_loss">stop-loss</Term>).

The same swap can cost wildly different amounts depending on which one you pick. That choice is one of the biggest hidden edges in trading - and one of the fastest ways beginners get bled.

Simply put: a market order is impatience, a limit order is patience, a stop-loss is a seatbelt.

- **Market order** - execute immediately against whatever is available. It will fill, but never at a price you can count on. You are the taker.
- **Limit order** - I will only buy at $X or lower, or sell at $Y or higher. You might wait forever, but you never pay more than you chose. You are the maker.
- **Stop order** - a trigger. It sleeps until price hits your level, then fires a market or limit order. This is how you get out of a losing position without watching the chart all day.

The trap we see most: people fire market orders into thin markets and get filled far from the price on screen. That silent gap is <Term id="slippage">slippage</Term>, and it is the number-one tax on impatient traders.
hints: Think of it as a restaurant: a market order is 'bring me whatever is fastest', a limit order is 'I'll wait for the exact dish I ordered'.
Pros almost never market-buy illiquid tokens. They post a limit and let the market come to them.

steps.title: Maker vs Taker: The Fee That Rewards Patience
steps.body:
Order books charge two different fees, and the gap between them is the whole game.

- A **market order** crosses the <Term id="spread">spread</Term> and removes liquidity. You are a *taker*, so you pay the taker fee - on major venues that is 0.05% to 0.10%.
- A **limit order** that sits in the book and waits *provides* liquidity. You are a *maker*, so you often pay a lower fee, or even receive a small rebate.

Run the numbers on a $10,000 trade:

1. Market order at 0.10% taker = **$10** in fees.
2. Resting limit order at 0.02% maker = **$2** in fees.
3. On top of that, the market order also eats the <Term id="bid_ask">bid/ask</Term> spread on every fill.

Over 100 trades, the patient trader quietly keeps an extra few hundred dollars - not by predicting price, but by choosing the right order type. That is why market makers exist: they get paid to *be* the limit orders everyone else trades against.
hints: Rule of thumb: if you are not in a hurry, you pay 2x-10x less by posting a limit order.
Stop-losses typically fire as market orders, so they pay the taker fee at the worst possible moment. Size them so the cost is acceptable.

steps.title: Under the Hood: How an Order Actually Fills
steps.body:
An <Term id="order_book">order book</Term> is just two sorted lists. **Bids** (buyers) sit stacked below the price; **asks** (sellers) sit stacked above it. The gap between the best bid and best ask is the spread.

When you send a market order, the matching engine walks the book level by level:

- It fills your first units at the **best** price.
- If your size exceeds that level, it keeps eating deeper levels at **worse** prices.
- Your *average* fill = total cost divided by total units. That average is where slippage shows up.

A limit order behaves differently: if it cannot fill immediately at your price, it **rests on the book** until someone crosses into it. At that moment you become the maker and earn the better fee.

Stop orders are just triggers, not magic. The engine watches the market; when the trigger price prints, it submits a live order. In a fast crash, price can gap *through* your stop and fill much lower - the famous stop-loss hunt everyone complains about. A stop guarantees you *try* to exit, not the price you exit at. That one distinction has saved and ruined more accounts than any indicator ever made.
hints: Deeper liquidity = less slippage on a market order. Check depth before you size up.
Stops are not free insurance. They cost the taker fee and can slip in volatile moves.

questions.prompt: You need to be in a token RIGHT NOW and the book is thin. You hit 'market buy'. What are you actually guaranteed?
options: A guaranteed fill, but not a guaranteed price
A guaranteed price, but not a guaranteed fill
Both price and fill are guaranteed by the exchange
Neither price nor fill is guaranteed
questions.explainRight: A market order always fills because it takes whatever liquidity exists - but in a thin book it walks down through worse and worse levels, so your average price can be far from the quote you saw. Fill is certain; price is not.
questions.explainWrong: Flip it: a market order sacrifices price to guarantee execution. You WILL get filled, but the price is whatever the book offers at that instant. If you want price certainty, you need a limit order - and then you accept that you might not fill at all.

questions.prompt: Why can posting a limit order cost you LESS in fees than a market order?
options: Limit orders are always hidden from the fee system
A resting limit order adds liquidity (maker), so venues charge a lower maker fee or pay a rebate
The exchange refunds limit orders because they are riskier
Limit orders do not pay any fee on any venue
questions.explainRight: Exchanges pay for liquidity. If your order sits in the book and someone else trades against it, you PROVIDED liquidity - you are a maker and get the cheaper (or rebated) fee. A market order TAKES liquidity and pays the taker fee.
questions.explainWrong: It is about who provides liquidity. A resting limit order supplies the book (maker, cheaper or rebated fee). A market order consumes the book (taker, more expensive fee). Limit orders still pay fees on real venues - they are just cheaper.

questions.prompt: Price is crashing hard. You had a stop-loss set 3% below entry, but it filled 9% below entry. What most likely happened?
options: A stop is only a TRIGGER; once fired it becomes a market order that can slip badly through levels in a fast move
Stops always fill exactly at the trigger price, so this is impossible
Limit orders are faster than market orders in a crash
questions.explainRight: Your stop woke up the moment price touched -3%, then submitted a live (usually market) order. In a violent candle the book can gap past your level, so you fill wherever liquidity actually sits. The stop guaranteed an attempt to exit, not the price - that is slippage through the stop.
questions.explainWrong: A stop-loss is a trigger, not a price guarantee. In a fast crash, price can gap through your level and your stop converts into a market order that slips. This is exactly why traders also use stop-limits and size positions so a bad fill is survivable.

questions.prompt: You want to buy a low-liquidity meme coin without moving the price against yourself. Which approach best matches the lesson?
options: Fire a large market order and accept whatever you get - speed is everything
Post a limit order inside the spread and let sellers come to you, plus split the size over time
Set a stop-loss above the current price so it buys on the way up
Always use market orders because they have lower fees
questions.explainRight: In a thin market, a big market order is how you get sandwiched and slip. Posting a limit order makes you the maker (better fee), avoids crossing deep levels, and splitting the size hides your intent. Patience is the edge.
questions.explainWrong: In thin markets, big market orders slip and get front-run (sandwiched). The patient play is a resting limit order inside the spread, often broken into smaller clips - you provide liquidity and pay the maker fee instead of bleeding the taker fee and spread.
